planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring in full sun to light shade, in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; install a deep rhizome barrier before planting since this running species spreads quickly.

directions: Phyllostachys rubromarginata is one of the fastest-growing temperate running bamboos, valued for its straight, thick-walled culms and the reddish blush that appears on new shoots and emerging leaves, which is the source of its common name. It tolerates alkaline soils and windy sites better than many Phyllostachys, and it is exceptionally cold hardy, holding up to temperatures well below zero once established. Because it is a monopodial runner, it needs a buried rhizome barrier or generous isolation to prevent it from invading nearby beds or neighboring yards. Harvest spring shoots for eating when they are a few inches above the soil, and thin older culms every few years to keep groves vigorous and to harvest poles for garden stakes or building projects.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil; roots survive well below zero even when top growth is killed back in the coldest winters, so a barrier is still needed to control spread.

directions: Phyllostachys nuda is among the most cold-tolerant of all timber bamboos, with rhizomes that can survive extreme winter lows even where top growth dies back, making it a good running-bamboo choice for gardeners at the cold edge of bamboo culture. Culms are a dark, glossy green with a distinctive pale ring below each node, and mature groves reach a moderate height compared to giant timber species, staying more manageable in smaller landscapes. The spring shoots are considered outstanding for eating, with a sweet flavor and low bitterness, and should be cut just below the soil surface while still short. Because it spreads by rhizome like all Phyllostachys, install a barrier or plan for regular rhizome pruning to keep the grove contained.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun to part shade in fertile, well-drained soil; install a deep rhizome barrier since it runs like other Phyllostachys.

directions: Robert Young bamboo is grown chiefly for its striking culms, which mature from pea-green with dark speckled sheaths to a rich butter-yellow randomly streaked with dark green stripes, making it a standout specimen or accent planting rather than an anonymous screen. It is a vigorous, cold-tolerant running form of Phyllostachys viridis that produces tall, arching canes and dense foliage capable of forming an effective privacy screen once established. Give it wind protection while young, since new culms can be somewhat brittle before they harden off, and keep soil consistently moist through the first two growing seasons. As with all running bamboos, a rhizome barrier is essential to prevent it from colonizing neighboring garden beds or lawns.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained, mulched soil; this clumping species needs no barrier and can be planted close to structures or property lines.

directions: Slender Weaver's Bamboo forms a tight, non-invasive clump of thin, upright, closely spaced culms topped with fine, weeping foliage, making it one of the most popular hedge and screening bamboos in warm-climate landscapes. Because its pachymorph rhizomes stay close to the base of the plant, it can be sited near fences, driveways, or property lines without the containment measures a running bamboo would require. It grows quickly once established, often reaching full screening height within two growing seasons, and appreciates regular moisture and a thick mulch layer to keep roots cool in hot summers. It is best suited to warm-temperate and subtropical gardens, since hard freezes will damage or kill top growth.

subcategory: clumping tropical timber and edible-shoot bamboo

planting.note: Plant container divisions or tissue-culture plants in spring after all danger of frost in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; this large tropical clumper needs ample room and consistent warmth.

directions: Beema bamboo forms massive, densely packed clumps of thick-walled culms armed with short thorny branches near the base, and it is among the fastest-growing bamboos in the world under warm, humid conditions. It is grown throughout South Asia for timber, construction poles, paper pulp, and biomass, and the young shoots are also harvested and cooked as a vegetable in parts of its native range. Because it is strictly tropical and frost sensitive, it is only appropriate for USDA zone 9b and warmer, and young plants should be protected from any cold snap during establishment. Give it generous space, deep fertile soil, and steady moisture, since mature clumps become extremely large and heavy over time.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in partial shade to morning sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; site with some shelter from harsh afternoon sun to preserve leaf color.

directions: This selection is prized above other Fargesia forms for its dramatic new culms, which emerge green and progress through red-purple to a pale orange as they age, giving established clumps a multicolored, painterly look in the garden. Like other Fargesia, it forms a tight, non-running clump and never spreads aggressively, so it is well suited to smaller gardens, foundation plantings, and mixed borders where a running bamboo would be unwelcome. It performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade, since the delicate leaves can scorch in intense summer heat, and it benefits from a consistent watering schedule during dry spells. It is one of the hardier ornamental clumping bamboos, tolerating winter cold well below zero once established.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; well suited to large containers as well as garden beds.

directions: Bimbo is the smallest-growing selection of Fargesia murielae, staying compact enough for small gardens, foundation beds, and large patio containers where a full-size umbrella bamboo would quickly overwhelm the space. It forms slender, upright, yellow-green canes clothed in fine, arching foliage, keeping the same graceful fountain form as its larger parent on a miniature scale. Like other Fargesia, it is a true non-running clumper, so it can be planted without root barriers or concern about spreading into lawns or neighboring beds. Give it part shade and steady moisture, especially in warmer zones, since it is happiest where summer heat is moderated and soil never fully dries out.
